countries.name: United States
countries.foreigners: Yes, but citizenship uncertainty since Aug 2026
countries.parentage: Pre-birth or post-birth parentage orders, depending on the state
countries.key_law: State statutes and case law (e.g. California Family Code 7960-7962, New York Child-Parent Security Act 2021, Michigan statute effective 1 April 2025)
countries.recent: 6 Aug 2026: executive orders seek to deny federal recognition of citizenship in some commercial-surrogacy births to non-citizen parents; court challenges filed and guidance pending. 1 Jul 2026: Florida's FIRE Act bars parties who are citizens or residents of seven 'foreign countries of concern'. 30 Jun 2026: Supreme Court upheld birthright citizenship in Trump v. Barbara.
countries.risk: Low for US residents; Medium for foreign parents
countries.summary: The most established destination. Most states allow compensated gestational surrogacy with court orders naming the intended parents. Louisiana restricts compensation, and a handful of states treat contracts as void or unenforceable even though surrogacy happens there. Foreign intended parents should get US immigration advice before starting because of the August 2026 executive orders.

countries.name: Canada
countries.parentage: Provincial: declaration or court order after birth (rules vary by province; Quebec has its own framework since 2023)
countries.key_law: Assisted Human Reproduction Act 2004, s.6; Reimbursement Related to AHR Regulations (2020)
countries.recent: Quebec created a regulated surrogacy framework in 2023 (notarised agreement before pregnancy). Federal rules unchanged.
countries.summary: Surrogacy is legal only on an altruistic basis. Paying a surrogate, paying anyone to arrange a surrogate's services, or advertising either is a federal offence (up to C$500,000 and/or 10 years). Surrogates can be reimbursed for receipted pregnancy-related expenses. Demand far exceeds the number of surrogates, so matching can take a year or more.

countries.name: Mexico
countries.parentage: Often a court process (amparo) after birth; registries apply rules inconsistently
countries.key_law: No federal law. Tabasco and Sinaloa regulate; Queretaro, Coahuila and San Luis Potosi prohibit; most states are silent. Supreme Court rulings (2021) recognised surrogacy and struck down Tabasco's exclusions.
countries.recent: Supreme Court decisions continue to shape practice state by state; no federal statute as of late 2026.
countries.summary: A popular lower-cost option, especially in Mexico City and Cancun, but the legal footing is court-made and uneven between states. Expect DNA tests and court steps to finalise parentage, and get advice from both a Mexican lawyer and a lawyer in your home country.

countries.name: Colombia
countries.key_law: No statute. Constitutional Court ruling T-968/2009 and later rulings urging Congress to legislate.
countries.recent: Aug 2026: bill PL 215/2026 filed to prohibit surrogacy. Sep 2025: new Health Ministry rules on importing and exporting gametes and embryos, after which a major Bogota provider stopped recruiting surrogates.
countries.summary: Surrogacy happens under court-recognised principles rather than a law. A 2026 bill would ban it. Anyone starting now should plan for the possibility that the rules change before the baby is born.

countries.name: Argentina
countries.parentage: Court-dependent; serious parentage risk after a 2024 Supreme Court ruling
countries.key_law: Civil and Commercial Code (no specific regulation)
countries.recent: Feb 2026: Australian government warned its citizens against surrogacy in Argentina.
countries.summary: Not prohibited, not regulated. Courts decide case by case, and recent rulings and foreign-government warnings make it a high-risk destination for international intended parents.

countries.name: Brazil
countries.key_law: Federal Council of Medicine resolutions: surrogate generally a relative (up to 4th degree)
countries.recent: No major change reported in 2025-2026.
countries.summary: Only altruistic surrogacy is allowed, normally with a relative as the surrogate, under medical-council rules rather than a statute.

countries.name: Chile
countries.parentage: Birth mother is the legal mother
countries.recent: Jan 2026: a congressional committee advanced a bill to criminalise both commercial and altruistic surrogacy.
countries.summary: No legal framework, and lawmakers are moving toward a ban.

countries.name: Cuba
countries.parentage: Court authorisation under the Family Code
countries.summary: The 2022 Family Code allows altruistic 'solidarity gestation', typically between relatives or close people, with court approval.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.parentage: Surrogate is legal mother at birth; parental order transfers parenthood
countries.key_law: Surrogacy Arrangements Act 1985; Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 2008
countries.recent: Sep 2026: government again declined to bring forward the Law Commission's 2023 reform proposals after a petition debate.
countries.risk: Low (legal), surrogate can change her mind before the order
countries.summary: Legal but altruistic: surrogates can receive reasonable expenses (often around GBP 10,000-15,000), agreements are not enforceable, and commercial agencies are banned. Intended parents apply for a parental order after the birth.

countries.name: Ireland
countries.parentage: Currently via guardianship/court routes; new statutory routes pending
countries.key_law: Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024 (largely not yet commenced)
countries.recent: 20 Apr 2026: section 232 commenced (parentage for some donor-conceived families). Regulator AHRRA established Oct 2025; surrogacy provisions still awaiting commencement and amendment.
countries.summary: Ireland passed a comprehensive law in 2024 that will allow regulated altruistic domestic surrogacy, but most of it is not in force yet. International surrogacy provisions are being reworked.

countries.name: Greece
countries.parentage: Court authorisation before transfer; intended parents named at birth
countries.key_law: Civil Code art. 1458; Law 3305/2005; Law 5197/2025 art. 46
countries.recent: May 2025: intended mother and surrogate must both be legal residents of Greece; single men and male couples excluded.
countries.summary: Once a destination for Europeans, Greece now restricts court-approved altruistic surrogacy to residents and excludes men without a female partner.

countries.name: Cyprus
countries.parentage: Prior approval by the national council
countries.recent: Northern Cyprus operates outside this framework with no official oversight.
countries.summary: Altruistic surrogacy with prior administrative approval for heterosexual couples and single women with a medical need.

countries.name: Portugal
countries.recent: Implementing rules still not in force.
countries.summary: Altruistic surrogacy exists on paper for women with specific medical conditions, but the system has not become operational.

countries.name: Spain
countries.parentage: Abroad: genetic parent can register; non-genetic parent must adopt
countries.recent: Feb 2026: prosecutors sought action against websites of 13 international agencies advertising to Spanish residents. Apr 2025: registries stopped accepting foreign birth certificates or court orders for surrogacy births.
countries.summary: Surrogacy contracts are void in Spain. Since 2025, Spanish families created abroad must establish parentage through biology or adoption rather than foreign court orders.

countries.name: France
countries.summary: All surrogacy agreements are void.

countries.name: Germany
countries.parentage: Birth mother is the legal mother; recognition of foreign orders case by case
countries.key_law: Embryo Protection Act 1990; Adoption Placement Act
countries.summary: Doctors may not assist surrogacy and arranging it is an offence. Germans who use surrogacy abroad often need court recognition or adoption at home.

countries.name: Italy
countries.recent: Oct 2024: surrogacy became prosecutable even when Italian citizens do it abroad.
countries.summary: Banned at home and, since 2024, a crime for Italians who arrange it anywhere in the world.

countries.name: Switzerland
countries.summary: Prohibited by the constitution; arrangers and clinicians can be punished.

countries.name: Austria
countries.summary: Commercial and altruistic surrogacy are both prohibited.

countries.name: Netherlands
countries.key_law: Criminal Code bans commercial arranging and advertising
countries.recent: Reform bill to regulate parentage pending.
countries.summary: Altruistic surrogacy is legal but very few clinics take part; commercial intermediaries and advertising are criminal.

countries.name: Belgium
countries.summary: No law; a few hospitals offer altruistic arrangements, and agreements have no legal force.

countries.name: Czech Republic
countries.parentage: Birth mother is legal mother; transfer is complex
countries.summary: Not regulated. The woman who gives birth is the legal mother, so transferring parenthood is legally complicated.

countries.name: Slovakia
countries.recent: Sep 2025: constitutional amendment prohibits surrogacy.
countries.summary: Banned by a 2025 constitutional amendment.

countries.name: Sweden
countries.summary: Not available in Swedish healthcare; Swedes who use surrogacy abroad must establish parentage at home.

countries.name: Norway
countries.summary: Surrogacy is not permitted.

countries.name: Finland
countries.summary: Both commercial and altruistic surrogacy have been banned since 2007.

countries.name: Ukraine
countries.parentage: Intended parents named on the birth certificate (Family Code art. 123)
countries.recent: Feb 2026: a large international agency filed for bankruptcy and its Kyiv clinic closed. The war continues to cause consular delays and travel risk.
countries.summary: Legally one of the clearest frameworks for married heterosexual couples with a medical indication, but the war makes it a very high-risk choice.

countries.name: Russia
countries.recent: Dec 2022: foreigners barred (except some married to Russian citizens).
countries.summary: Commercial surrogacy remains available to Russian citizens with a medical indication; foreign intended parents were excluded in 2022.

countries.name: Georgia
countries.parentage: Intended parents named on the birth certificate
countries.key_law: Law on Health Care (1997) and Civil Registry rules
countries.recent: Oct 2026: a major clinic partnership ended and reported waits grew to as long as three years. A 2023 plan to ban surrogacy for foreigners stalled; 2025 trafficking investigations involved surrogates recruited from abroad.
countries.summary: Compensated surrogacy is legal for married heterosexual couples with infertility, and foreigners can still access it. A ban for foreigners has been proposed before, and investigations into abuse of surrogates in 2025 raise serious ethical questions.

countries.name: Armenia
countries.summary: Paid surrogacy is permitted and used by some foreign couples, with limited regulatory oversight.

countries.name: Kazakhstan
countries.recent: 26 Jul 2026: amendment signed limiting surrogacy to legally married Kazakh citizens.
countries.summary: Closed to foreigners in 2026 after an inquiry into exploitation and illegal donor networks.

countries.name: Kyrgyzstan
countries.summary: Paid surrogacy is permitted with light regulation.

countries.name: Israel
countries.recent: 2022: access extended to same-sex couples and single men.
countries.summary: Regulated by a state approvals committee for Israeli residents, including same-sex couples and single men since 2022.

countries.name: United Arab Emirates
countries.parentage: Abu Dhabi framework recognises the intended parents
countries.key_law: Federal Decree-Law No. 17 of 2023 (removed the ban); Abu Dhabi DoH Gestational Surrogacy Standard
countries.recent: Sep 2023: federal reform removed the explicit ban and left regulation to each emirate. Abu Dhabi has since issued a Gestational Surrogacy Standard (revised 2025); the first publicised births under it were reported in Nov 2026.
countries.summary: The 2023 federal reform removed the old ban and left regulation to each emirate. Abu Dhabi now licenses gestational surrogacy for married couples living in the UAE using their own eggs and sperm; other emirates have not published equivalent rules.

countries.name: South Africa
countries.parentage: High Court confirms the agreement before conception
countries.summary: Altruistic surrogacy with court approval before conception; at least one commissioning parent must live in South Africa.

countries.name: Nigeria
countries.summary: No specific legislation; practice exists with significant legal uncertainty.

countries.name: Kenya
countries.parentage: Surrogate is legal mother; adoption petitions needed
countries.key_law: No specific law (2024 High Court noted the gap)
countries.recent: 2024: High Court acknowledged the legislative gap.
countries.summary: No statute; parents usually need post-birth adoption, which creates travel and status uncertainty.

countries.name: India
countries.parentage: Child is legally the intended couple's at birth
countries.recent: Feb 2024: donor gametes allowed where a partner has a medical condition. Advertising commercial surrogacy is an offence (up to 10 years).
countries.summary: Only altruistic surrogacy for Indian married couples with proven infertility (and some widowed or divorced women), with certificates from authorities. Commercial surrogacy, and advertising it, are criminal offences.

countries.name: Thailand
countries.foreigners: Only if married to a Thai national (reform pending)
countries.parentage: Intended parents recognised under the 2015 Act
countries.key_law: Protection of Children Born through Assisted Reproductive Technologies Act 2015
countries.recent: Jul 2026: public consultation on a revised bill to admit foreign married couples, including same-sex couples, where the surrogate shares a spouse's nationality. Commercial surrogacy stays banned.
countries.summary: Altruistic surrogacy for married couples where at least one spouse is Thai. A 2026 draft would widen access, but commercial surrogacy remains a crime.

countries.name: Vietnam
countries.key_law: Law on Marriage and Family 2014 (in force 2015)
countries.summary: Humanitarian surrogacy only, for married couples, with a relative as surrogate.

countries.name: China
countries.summary: Medical institutions may not perform surrogacy.

countries.name: Japan
countries.key_law: No statute; medical society guidelines discourage it
countries.summary: No law, but professional guidelines mean it is practically unavailable.

countries.name: Cambodia
countries.summary: Commercial surrogacy was banned in 2016 after a boom in foreign demand.

countries.name: Nepal
countries.summary: Surrogacy has been halted since a 2015 Supreme Court order.

countries.name: Malaysia
countries.summary: Not permitted.

countries.name: Philippines
countries.key_law: No framework; professional society bars members from assisting
countries.summary: No legal framework, and the national reproductive-medicine society bars its members from helping.

countries.name: Australia
countries.parentage: Parentage order from a state court after birth
countries.key_law: State and territory surrogacy Acts (Northern Territory joined in 2022)
countries.recent: 2026: the Australian Law Reform Commission is reviewing surrogacy laws, including whether surrogates should be compensated. Commercial surrogacy remains a criminal offence; NSW, Queensland and the ACT also criminalise residents arranging it overseas.
countries.summary: Every state and territory allows altruistic surrogacy with counselling, legal advice and a court order after birth. Commercial surrogacy is a crime, including overseas for residents of some states.

countries.name: New Zealand
countries.summary: Altruistic surrogacy with ethics-committee approval for clinic-assisted cases; parents adopt after the birth.

status_explain.compensated: Surrogates may be paid beyond expenses under the law, usually with eligibility rules.
status_explain.varies: Rules depend on the state or region (United States, Mexico).
status_explain.altruistic: Only documented expenses may be reimbursed; payment or paid brokering is prohibited.
status_explain.residents: Regulated, but only for citizens or residents who meet set conditions.
status_explain.unregulated: No specific law; courts decide case by case, so outcomes are uncertain.
status_explain.prohibited: Surrogacy agreements are banned or void; some countries also penalise arranging it abroad.
